column4: I spoke a word of the old language, and the sleeping statue opened its eyes.
A parrot twisted its tongue around the words until it could talk like the station announcer.
A vendor made it a rule to sell a letter only after the buyer could read its words aloud.
Before the bats woke, the explorer wrote down the cave’s echoes in her own words.
After enduring an hour of speeches, a boy perked up when he began to recognize words from his grandmother's lullaby.
A sign spelled out which direction to go to visit the lighthouse that sang in the fog.
At noon, the head librarian said the words that would permit the tortoise to borrow its first book.
The surveyor spoke the numbers aloud to measure ten paces in the dark tunnel.
The final word of the lesson made a pear fall out of the chalkboard.
A farmer stretched a slender thread across the rice field, and a mouse used it as a tightrope.
A sailor used red thread to tie a good-luck charm to the mast.
At the club meeting, every member brought a different color of thread to sew a picture of the village.
An apprentice could reach the next rank by spinning a thread long enough to cross the hall.
A horse used a ruler to mark where the platform of the train station ought to end.
The horse played a musical phrase on the piano each time the pony tapped its hoof.
The sun saw a patch of blue over the harbor and decided the weather could finally clear up.
When the sun disappeared, the sound of a single cricket filled the darkness.
A mirror at the center of the plaza could reflect the sun onto every balcony at once.
A pheasant circled the sun once for each day—Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday—so the village could count the full week.
At dawn, a cook bought a cut of meat for a stew she swore would give her the guts to sing in public.
A fox hung a slice of liver out to dry, and the piece of flesh grew two tiny wings.
A tiny door rested on the giant's shoulder; when he lifted his arm, its hinge pressed into the flesh beneath it.
A girl pointed a finger at the delicious cake, and the baker put the last piece in her hand.
A child drew the parcel into an embrace when two tiny hands reached out of it.
A knight used one hand to push a suit of armor through the revolving door.
A clockmaker used her bare hand to strike a bell loud enough to wake the whole block.
A juggler used one hand to throw a toy spear so high that a cloud caught it.
A customer put her hand through a private booth's curtain to pay for a secret fortune.
When the white curtains lifted, every pair of hands began to clap for the acrobats.
She reached out a hand to pick one of the dice, and it landed on seven.
A student held out both hands to receive the key that would grant access to the tower.
A queen summoned her jester by using one hand to beckon him out of a painting.
When the last two pieces fit together, an enormous hand reached down to pick up the puzzle.
The mayor decided to plant the tree straight after a crooked one walked away on its roots.
A tree split in a storm, and the carpenter used the piece that fell east to make the ridgepole.
In the toy army's war, a single tin spear served as a bridge over the moat.
A locksmith dropped two keys made from the same metal in a fountain and came back to find copper-colored fish.
At the end of the passage, a metal mirror showed every visitor wearing an enormous crown.
A seedling of grass sprouted in the rice field and grew high enough to hide a heron.
A walker carried a statue's missing head down the road to the museum in a shopping basket.
